name: SWE-Gym
description: SWE-Gym is the first environment for training software engineering (SWE) agents. It contains 2,438 real-world task instances, each comprising a Python codebase with an executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a task specified in natural language. The dataset is sourced from pull requests in 11 popular Python repositories, with pre-configured executable environments and expert-validated test cases, constructed in close alignment with SWE-Bench. It also includes SWE-Gym Lite (230 instances) for rapid prototyping and SWE-Gym Raw (64,689 instances spanning 358 Python repositories) without executable environments.
creator: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang
publisher: PMLR (Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning)
citeAs: Pan, J., Wang, X., Neubig, G., Jaitly, N., Ji, H., Suhr, A., & Zhang, Y. (2025). Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym. Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267.
rai:dataCollection: SWE-Gym was constructed by first using SEART GitHub search to filter repositories created before July 1, 2022 with more than 500 stars, at least 300 lines of code, more than 500 pull requests, and 100 contributors. Task instances were extracted from GitHub pull requests using SWE-Bench's instance extraction script. Executable environments were manually configured for 11 repositories, requiring approximately 200 human annotation hours and 10,000 CPU core hours. Instances were validated using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure gold patches pass more unit tests than the original code.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Instances that failed environment setup validation were filtered out. The process of manually configuring dependencies for specific codebase versions was challenging due to backward compatibility issues, especially for older GitHub issues, which may have led to some instances being excluded.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real-world GitHub issues and pull requests from 358 Python repositories (for SWE-Gym Raw) and 11 popular Python repositories (for SWE-Gym), including natural language issue descriptions, repository snapshots, and unit tests. The repositories were identified via SEART GitHub search.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Repositories created before July 1, 2022 were included. The dataset construction process is described as occurring prior to publication in 2025.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Instances were associated with version numbers and environments were set up version-by-version to avoid redundant setup work. SWE-Bench's versioning script was generalized to support versioning via script execution. Dependencies were manually configured using configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at the time of issue creation. Pre-built Docker images were created for each instance for full reproducibility, totaling 6 TB.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: From 64,689 raw instances across 358 repositories, 11 repositories were selected for manual environment configuration. Instances were versioned and executable environments were set up. SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script was used to ensure gold patches pass more unit tests than the original code. Failed instances were filtered out, resulting in 2,438 validated instances. SWE-Gym Lite (230 instances) was created by following the SWE-Bench Lite filtering pipeline, excluding tasks requiring editing more than one file, tasks with poorly described problem statements, those with excessively complex ground-truth code diffs, and tests focused on error message validation.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations (executable environments and instance validation) were done by a subset of the authors, requiring approximately 200 human annotation hours. Agent trajectories were labeled as successful or unsuccessful based on whether the gold patch passes more unit tests than the original code, using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script. For verifier training, trajectories were labeled as successful (<YES>) or unsuccessful (<NO>) based on unit test outcomes.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: OpenHands remote runtime (for parallelizing evaluation and trajectory execution), Docker (for pre-built executable environments), SWE-Bench execution-based validation script
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The task success probability follows a long-tail distribution, where more samples increase solved instances but introduce bias toward easier tasks. Per-instance capping was introduced to mitigate this bias. A cap of 2 was found to achieve a good balance between dataset bias and size.
rai:annotatorDemographics: A subset of the paper's authors performed the manual annotation (approximately 200 human annotation hours).
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SWE-Bench instance extraction script, SWE-Bench execution-based validation script, SWE-Bench versioning script, SEART GitHub search, Docker, OpenHands remote runtime, SGLang, torchtune, Unsloth
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: SWE-Gym, models, agent trajectories, pre-built Docker images, and training pipeline are publicly released. The dataset is described as a foundation for future research. Future directions include automatic environment synthesis for expanding repository diversity, types of tasks, and programming languages.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Improving automated software engineering capabilities could increase developer productivity and accessibility across industries. As agents become more capable, they may impact software engineering jobs and require careful consideration around code ownership, licensing, and attribution. Similar techniques could potentially be misused to automate the creation of malicious code. The authors encourage future work to explore frameworks for responsible deployment, including considerations around security, safety, and economic impacts.
rai:dataBiases: Task distribution across repositories exhibits a long-tail pattern, with pandas comprising nearly one-third of total tasks and bokeh representing only one percent. Success probability follows a long-tail distribution biased toward easier tasks. Manual environment configuration may introduce distribution bias by excluding tasks with complex dependencies. Tasks in SWE-Gym are on average harder than those in SWE-Bench.
rai:dataLimitations: SWE-Gym is limited by its environment diversity, including the number of repositories (11 for the main dataset), types of tasks, and programming languages (Python only). The dataset currently contains 2,438 instances, and performance improvements are currently limited by compute budget for sampling rather than dataset size. Self-improvement results are modest. The gap between Pass@k and Best@k indicates room for improvement in reward modeling for coding agents.
rai:dataUseCases: Training language model-based software engineering agents via rejection sampling fine-tuning and reinforcement learning; training verifier (outcome-supervised reward) models for inference-time scaling; evaluating SWE agent performance; rapid prototyping with SWE-Gym Lite; future research in SWE agent development and automatic dataset synthesis with SWE-Gym Raw.
